Title: Antec India announces the availability of NeoECO C Series Power Supplies
URL: https://www.itvoice.in/antec-india-announces-the-availability-of-neoeco-c-series-power-supplies
Published: 2013-07-31T08:57:52.000Z
Author: Gupta Vikas
Highlights:
NEW DELHI / MUMBAI / BANGALORE, India – July 30, 2013

Antec Inc, a global leader in high-performance computer components and accessories for the gaming, PC upgrade and Do-It-Yourself markets, has added 520w and 620w, high efficient power supplies to its NeoECO C series, now available in the India market. Features like Industrial safety protection, including short circuit and over voltage protection, for stable and reliable power makes NeoECO C series unique as compared to generic power supplies.

Antec NEOECO C series provides economical power and comes with the features of quiet double ball bearing 120mm fan, universal input with active power factor correction (PFC) and meets 80 PLUS Bronze certification, the most widely recognized independent standard in energy efficiency. The NEOECO series allows the system to perform in a cooler and quieter way which is powered by Continuous Power. 

Kevan Li, Business Head – India at Antec Inc, said “The Antec NeoEco C Series power supplies are ideal for a smooth and valuable computing experience. When it comes to PC Power Supplies, consumers expect a solution which provides value for money and is efficient and reliable; the NeoEco C series PSUs fit the bill perfectly.”

##### Efficiency

80 Plus (trademarked 80 PLUS) is a voluntary certification program intended to promote efficient energy use in computer power supply units (PSUs). It certifies products that have more than 80% energy efficiency at 20%, 50% and 100% of rated load, and a power factor of 0.9 or greater at 100% load. Such PSUs waste 20% or less electric energy as heat at the specified load levels, reducing electricity use and bills compared to less efficient PSUs.

- Failed to meet the power sequencing criteria (V column showed a red circle). This was confirmed by looking at 5V and 3.3V rails by an oscilloscope. As you can see in the below screenshot, the 5V rail was greater than 3.3V for the first 500 microseconds. However, this is not a big issue as the voltage difference is small (<300mV) and the duration is very short (400 microseconds). This failure alone is not enough to render this PSU as faulty or not usable.
